To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the structure of a proteolytic Salmonella effector GtgE is solved, which will help understand its function in Salmonella infection.
GtgE is a protease that is active only in vivo, and its activity is stimulated by a factor(s) that is not present in the in vitro assays.
the crystal structure of a proteolytic fragment of GtgE reveals a papain-like active site, which is assembled in a catalytically inactive protein.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural basis of proteolytic activity of Salmonella GtgE and its potential role in the pathogenesis of Salmonella infections.
the structure of Gtge and its proteolytic activity.
the structural and biochemical characterization of GtgE and the identification of its substrates and protein partners.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the GtgE is a cysteine protease, which is not active in vitro, and its activity is stimulated in vivo by an unknown factor(s).
GtgE is a papain-like cysteine protease with low activity in vitro and that its function in vivo is dependent on other factors.
GtgE is a cysteine protease that is active on a subset of Rabs, but the mechanism and the nature of its activity are yet to be elucidated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
GtgE, like other effectors from the same family of Salmonella effector proteins (Sef), is an enzyme with a very specific activity.
GtgE is a papain-like cysteine protease with a novel mode of action.
GtgE is a papain-like cysteine protease that is active in vivo but not in vitro.
The main takeaway from our work is that
GtgE is the first example of a protease that is inactive in vitro but active in vivo.
the GtgE structure is a useful starting point for the design of GtgE constructs with improved activity.
